claims.text: The proposed target is a fully disordered, equiatomic high-entropy superconductor containing at least five elements, each above 5 at.%.
The superconducting transition temperature is primarily governed by average valence electron concentration.
Average valence electron concentration tunes the electronic density of states.
Changes in electronic density of states alter electron–phonon coupling.
Chemical disorder produces lattice distortions that modulate electron-scattering rates.
A controlled change in valence electron concentration without formation of secondary phases can systematically change Tc.
The target alloy is a single-phase Ti-rich heavy-transition-metal solid solution outside the well-studied Nb–Ta-dominated class.
Most previously studied type-A high-entropy-alloy superconductors contain large amounts of niobium and tantalum.
Replacing about 5 at.% of one constituent with a similarly sized element having a different valence electron count will preserve the disordered single-phase state.
The substitution will incrementally increase or decrease the alloy's average valence electron concentration.
The balance among density of states, electron–phonon coupling, local lattice strain, and electron scattering sets the observed Tc.
Increasing valence electron concentration will raise Tc relative to the baseline.
Decreasing valence electron concentration will lower Tc relative to the baseline.
The proposed mechanism applies only while the material remains a single-phase disordered solid solution without significant segregation or secondary precipitates.
A valence electron concentration of roughly 4–7 electrons is typical for metallic superconductors.
Disorder can suppress superconductivity near an Anderson quantum phase transition.
Five-species compositional disorder in a BCC HEA has been associated with superconductivity even when the corresponding binary component alloys were not superconducting above 2 K.
Failure of controlled VEC changes to produce a measurable systematic Tc change beyond experimental uncertainty would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The boundary states that the hypothesis applies only when no secondary phases form, whereas the falsification rule treats secondary-phase formation as falsifying the mechanism. Secondary phases would instead place the experiment outside the stated domain and confound, rather than decisively falsify, the hypothesis.
